Marblehead: The engine's #1 team went 6-6. That is not a mistake — Onawa Khan is the best head coach in Roiland at 9.62, the top-30 talent is the deepest anywhere, and four players still went to the draft. What stopped them last year is sitting in plain sight: a 3.98 defensive coordinator against a 7.96 on offense. They are a top-ten offense bolted to a bottom-third defense, and they drew the 31st-hardest schedule to prove it either way. The title drought runs to 1971.
Skeenerland State: Second in the country and no national championship in the program's history. The roster is why — Stanislaw Lesovec at 9.14, a 8.74 corner, a 8.68 linebacker, and only one player lost to the draft, the lightest bleed in the top five. They also won the portal, +6 in and 3 out, and signed four blue-chips in a six-man class. The worry is the staff: Shaojun Mingxia left the offensive coordinator's chair to take the Sacred Tomb job, and his 4.46 replacement is the weakest link on any top-five team.
Ranroman State: They ended Tengus State's season in the quarterfinals and then lost seven players to the draft, more than anyone else in the top ten. Halona Robinson is a 9.31 head coach and the offense is in good hands at 8.55, but the defense sits at 5.89 and the roster developed 78th in the league over the offseason — the worst mark of any top-five team. Seven blue-chips in a fourteen-man class says they know it. Their last title was 2034, which by Roiland standards is recent enough to make this feel like a window rather than a rebuild.
Ranroman: The most balanced staff in the country: 9.24 at head coach, 8.07 on offense, 8.10 on defense, with no weak chair anywhere. They signed seven blue-chips and every single member of their class was one — a seven-for-seven haul, the purest in the league. They lost only two to the draft. The drought is the story: no title since 1983, and this is the most complete roster they have fielded in that span.
Orlot: A quarterback and a receiver both above 9.0 — Eleanor Boispierre at 9.05 and Vladislav Ivanenko at 9.07 — which is the most dangerous passing combination in the top ten. The defensive coordinator is their best coach at 8.70, so for once the balance runs the right way. But they drew the fifth-hardest schedule in the country, and their last national title was 1969. Seven blue-chips arrive. If this group cannot do it, the roster that follows will not be better.
Diamond City: The best-developing roster in Roiland last offseason — first of 152 — under a head coach who was an interim a year ago and kept the job. Niana Sandgate went 2-0 in relief at Diamond City and the committee retained her; she is now 8.69 and running the league's most improved program. They lost nobody to the draft. The catch is a 3.20 offensive coordinator, the second-worst in the top 25, paired with a 7.97 on defense. Projected 9.1 wins, the third-highest figure on this list, off a 37th-ranked schedule.
Tengus State: The computer's #1 team all last season, and it bought them a one-point loss in the Power North final and a quarterfinal exit to a team that finished 5-4 in its own conference. Now they return the second-best developing roster in the league, a 9.10 defensive lineman, and a six-for-six blue-chip class. Layla Smith is only a 7.08 head coach but both coordinators are near 8. Projected 9.4 wins is the highest total in the top 25. Their last title was 2026 — the first year of the modern era, and a long time to be this good without another.
Kaji Daun: The only program in the country with all three coaches above 9.0 — 8.99, 9.01, 9.04 — which is why they developed fifth in the league and lost nobody at all to the draft. Edouard Lafort, Jalen Tingjing and Adaeze Kwanti all sit near 9.0. Then Otto Peatwell left the defensive coordinator's chair to take the Parchynt head job, and the 9.04 figure above is his replacement's number to live up to. Third-hardest schedule in Roiland. Last title 2032.
UNN: Kadhim Ugonse is a sophomore running back at 9.33, the fourth-best player in the country, and he is carrying a program that signed zero recruits this cycle — the class is literally empty, because the roster had no room. Three players left for the draft. The defensive coordinator is excellent at 8.84 and the head coach is solid, but the fourth-hardest schedule in the league against a projected 6.9 wins is the bleakest gap on this list. Last title 2018.
North Hatesei: Five and seven, and ranked tenth. The historical colossus of Roiland football has a 9.13 offensive coordinator, a 9.26 defensive coordinator, the third-best developing roster in the league, and an offensive lineman at 9.18. They also drew the single hardest schedule in the country. Seven blue-chips arrive. A program with more national titles than anyone does not stay 5-7 with this staff, and the schedule means we find out early.
Greene: A senior team. The top three — Ngaio Yremaw, Nikolaos Goldwick, Jadwiga Kirchbrandt — are all seniors, and so is most of what matters behind them. Seven blue-chips in a twelve-man class is the succession plan, but it is next year's plan. Seventh in development, ninth-hardest schedule, and a 2020 title that is starting to feel further away than it is. This is the last call for this group.
Kaji Kita: They won the Power North, beating Tengus State by a point in the final, and they have never won a national championship. Kalisi Lealelei and Sorei Ommirrei are both above 9.0 and both seniors. The problem is behind them: Kaji Kita developed 123rd of 152 over the offseason, with a 6.67 offensive coordinator and a 5.70 on defense doing the teaching. Twelve recruits, five blue-chips. The window is this year, because the staff is not building another one.
UN Ediville: Six and six with a 3-6 conference record, ranked thirteenth, which tells you how much talent is sitting on a disappointing record. Samira Harinathan is a 9.28 safety. Both coordinators are above 8.0 while the head coach is the weak chair at 6.87 — an unusual shape, and one that usually means a team plays better than it is led. Seven blue-chips in an eight-man class. Their 2033 title is the most recent on this half of the list.
Central Stanton: They have the best player in Roiland. Evangelos Fiorarini is a sophomore tight end at 9.95, the engine's hard ceiling, after a +1.55 jump that was the largest in the league — produced by a 9.43 offensive coordinator, the best in the country. The defense is a 5.39, and they drew the second-hardest schedule. Twelve wins and a Great Fourteen title last year; a three-man recruiting class, all blue-chips, this year. Everything about this team is lopsided and it keeps working.
Will Tech: From this season the Tasson game is week 10 and both programs sit idle the week before, which makes it the only fixture in Roiland with a bye built in front of it. Will Tech arrives with a 9.20 defensive lineman and a 9.17 senior quarterback, eighth-best development in the league — and a 4.06 defensive coordinator, because Digby Charlac left to take the Verigon State head job. Projected 8.9 wins. Last title 2002.
Eona: Ninety years. Eona last won a national championship in 1947, the longest drought of any team in this top 25 by four decades. The roster is quietly excellent — two defensive linemen at 9.01 and 8.66, a sophomore quarterback at 8.74, both coordinators at 8.07 and 8.08 — and they signed seven blue-chips in a seven-man class, every one of them. Eleventh-hardest schedule. Nobody is picking them, which is roughly how these things start.
Ciarralotta Tech: Fifteen and two, a national runner-up, and ranked seventeenth. The draft took five players including Ryskamp winner Xiaodan Sakaki, and what is left is a 2.56 offensive coordinator — the worst number on any ranked team and one of the worst in Roiland. Gwen Oberoi is a 9.12 head coach and the recruiting was strong, seven blue-chips. But they have never won a national title, they just came the closest they ever have, and the man who was going to throw them there has graduated.
Rogaela State: The defending champion, back-to-back, 16-1, ranked eighteenth. Eight players went to the draft — more than any other top-25 program — and that is the whole story: the roster that won consecutive titles has been taken apart by the league it beat. What remains is still good enough for a projected 9.3 wins, second-highest here, and they went +4 in the portal and signed seven blue-chips. Rami Campbell's staff is balanced at 7.9 across all three chairs. Nobody has won three straight since Greene in 1940.
Natzumakis: Five and seven, 2-7 in the Western Coast, ranked nineteenth — the biggest gap between record and rating on the board. They were the most aggressive team in the portal relative to their size, +5 and only one out, and Porfirio Zanetti left for the Stanton offensive coordinator job, leaving a 3.29 behind him. Sixtieth-hardest schedule is the kindest draw of anyone ranked. Last title 1972. This is a bet on talent that has not yet produced a result.
Parchynt: Otto Peatwell is the most interesting hire of the carousel: an 8.99 coordinator who ran Kaji Daun's defense, now a first-time head coach at a program that has never won a national title. He inherits a roster that lost nobody to the draft, went +2 in the portal, and ranks twentieth with a 58th-ranked schedule. Three recruits, two blue-chips, which is thin. The ceiling here is entirely about whether a great coordinator becomes a great head coach.
Dietsche: Sora Yamamoto is an 8.98 head coach watching his offense run through a 2.94 coordinator, after Mathis Ravendale left to take the Leafette head job. That is the single steepest drop-off any ranked team is carrying. The roster is young — a sophomore receiver and a sophomore kicker lead it — and they went +3 in the portal. Easiest schedule of anyone ranked at 74th. Last title 2019, which is recent enough that the fans remember exactly what this is supposed to look like.
Hatesei: Tuva Kessler is a 8.97 senior tight end on a team whose defensive coordinator is a 2.57 — the worst number on the board, after Hwanki Ji left to coordinate Ranroman State's offense. They developed 91st, drew the sixth-hardest schedule, and are projected for 5.4 wins, the lowest figure of any ranked team. Fifteen recruits with seven blue-chips is a real class. It is also a class that will not help until the defense has somebody to teach it. Last title 1986.
Stanton: Shamar Raptis arrives from Riveral's offensive coordinator chair as a 4.91 head coach, the lowest-rated man leading any ranked program. He inherits Chinedu Okozie, a senior receiver at 9.69 and the second-best player in Roiland, a 7.90 and a 7.98 in the coordinator chairs, and a roster that lost nobody at all to the draft. Eighteenth in development, twelfth-hardest schedule, four blue-chips. A good roster and an unproven voice. Last title 2022.
Eternal Fox: Thirteen and two, an East Forest title, and the 116th-hardest schedule in Roiland — by far the softest draw of any ranked team, and the honest reason they are ranked twenty-fourth instead of top ten. Seven players went to the draft and the roster developed 89th. Jian Wright left Eternal Fox for the Stanton job during the carousel, and the staff behind him sits at 6.68 and 7.15. Fifteen recruits with only three blue-chips. Last title 1984. The record will likely look excellent again; the question is whether it will mean anything in December.
South Antiragal: Six transfers in and one out, the biggest portal haul of any ranked team, built around Ebony Yawchukwu, a senior quarterback at 8.62, and two corners above 8.2. Rhys Fontenot is a strong 8.48 head coach with a 4.92 defensive coordinator underneath him. Fifty-ninth-ranked schedule and a projected 7.1 wins. Last title 1990. This is a roster assembled rather than grown, which in Roiland usually means one very good year or none at all.
